ITBS is a compression syndrome provoked by repeated cycling through roughly 20-30 degrees of knee flexion under load, and its diagnostic signature is pain that appears during activity and worsens with duration rather than warming up. A band that is sore to press 48 hours after roughly 1990m of descent is reporting tissue sensitivity, which is the expected consequence of that load rather than evidence of the syndrome. Firing the downgrade on this would cost a real session on evidence that does not support it. The surface argument is the reason this is worth 10 load points rather than a hazard. Soft dry sand yields under the foot and absorbs most of the impact-braking cycle, so a sand descent is a fraction of the band provocation of the same vertical drop on a trail; it is close to free eccentric exposure for an ITB history, which is precisely what ordinary descent is not. 300m is deliberately small, roughly a quarter of 22 August's descent and a quarter of the 5 September cap, so the eccentric ramp across the flat fortnight stays gently positive from a near-zero base rather than spiking. reason: The 23 August entry set the race target at 60 g/h and named one unresolved input: whether the athlete's products were single-transporter or glucose-fructose blends, since 90 g/h requires blends to clear the roughly 60 g/h SGLT1 glucose ceiling. That input is now answered and the assumption behind the 60 was wrong in the athlete's favour. Enervit Carbo Gel C2:1 Pro is 40g of carbohydrate per 60ml gel at a 2:1 glucose-fructose ratio: roughly double the density of a typical gel and already the correct transporter profile. Two gels an hour is 80 g/h at about 53g glucose and 27g fructose, which sits inside both the ~60 g/h glucose and ~30-35 g/h fructose ceilings with margin, so 80 is not a stretch target but the natural operating point of the product he already owns. The 22 August intake is now reconstructed exactly rather than estimated: 2 Carbo Gels plus 1 SiS is 102g from gels over 5h08, about 20 g/h, and roughly 25 g/h including the bar, which confirms the earlier 21-29 g/h estimate and confirms that the failure was delivery rather than tolerance. He was carrying the right product and taking a third of it. Three specifics are now written into the sessions because each is a distinct failure mode. First, the SiS GO Isotonic is 22g of maltodextrin with 10mg of sodium, glucose pathway only; added on top of two Carbo Gels it takes hourly glucose to about 75g, past the transport ceiling, and the surplus ferments in the gut. It is excluded from the high-intake plan rather than merely deprioritised. Second, 40g in 60ml is roughly a 66% solution and strongly hypertonic, so it draws water into the lumen if taken without fluid; 150-250ml per gel is prescribed as a rule, and this is named as the single most likely cause if 29 August goes badly. His 487 ml/h on 22 August is already the right volume, it simply has to be timed to the gels. Third, the Bulk Complete Electrolyte Powder carries no carbohydrate at all, which invalidates the 23 August instruction to put carbohydrate in the bottle: his bottle was a carrier and never a fuel source. Its 1g scoop is sodium-chloride-first and therefore somewhere around 150-250mg of sodium, which cannot be verified from published data, so the session asks him to read the tub rather than asserting a number. The purchase recommendation is one product and it is chosen to add no new variables: Enervit Isocarb C2:1 Pro, 65g sachet in 500ml, 60g carbohydrate and 600mg sodium, same brand and same 2:1 ratio as the gel he tolerates. One sachet an hour plus one gel every second hour is 80 g/h with the sodium target met exactly and the solution isotonic rather than hypertonic. The logistics argument is what makes this more than a refinement: 80 g/h from gels alone over a 7h45 race is 16 gels, about 1.1kg and a litre of packaging, which is a plausible reason to under-fuel by hour five whatever the intention. The split system is 8 sachets and 4 gels. Sequencing is rate first then duration: 29 August is 1h45, short enough that jumping straight to 80 g/h from a 25 g/h baseline is low risk, and it isolates whether the concentration is tolerable. 5 September then tests whether it holds for four and a half hours, which is the observation that actually predicts hour six at Pirin. Race day already specified 70-90 g/h, so this change makes the training consistent with the race rather than changing the race. Confidence is high on the transporter arithmetic and on the product data, which is from the manufacturer's own nutrition panels. The genuine risk is that 80 g/h is a 3.2x increase on demonstrated intake with 19 days to adapt; the hedge is that the rate test comes 14 days out on a short flat run where failure is cheap and recoverable, and that a verified 65-70 g/h would still be a large improvement over 25 and is an acceptable landing point if 80 does not hold.

reason: This morning's read was tenderness to palpation and stretch only, and it was assessed as benign tissue sensitivity 48h after roughly 1990m of descent, at high confidence, with the 5 September contingency explicitly held rather than fired. That assessment is now wrong and is reversed on new information rather than defended. Intermittent pin sensations during walking are a categorically different observation: walking cycles the knee through the 20-30 degree flexion band under body weight, so symptoms there mean provocation at a load threshold well below running. The criteria I wrote this morning anticipated the next signal arriving from a run and set a positive Noble test or in-run pain as the trigger; the signal arrived from gait instead, which is a lower threshold and therefore a stronger signal, not a weaker one, so the contingency fires now rather than waiting for Thursday to confirm what walking already says. The decision is close to free and that is the whole argument. CTL is 43 against a target of 42, which the plan has already met, so there is no fitness left to acquire in 19 days and every remaining session is risk management or sharpening. Set against that, the asymmetry is severe: early ITBS responds to a short decisive deload, whereas established ITBS does not resolve inside 19 days, and this athlete has a documented March ITBS to show what the bad branch looks like. Spending three days of flat running now buys the start line; spending them to protect a week that was already designated as having no specific purpose buys nothing. The load is held rather than cut wherever possible, which is why the week goes to the bike instead of to rest: 365 against 410 keeps CTL essentially flat while removing every impact cycle, and the athlete has explicitly wanted the bike used for exactly this trade. Saddle raised 1-2cm and cadence 90-100 are prescribed because a low saddle and a big gear are the two ways a bike can drive the knee through more flexion under more force. Uphill running is preserved as the single exception and is worth stating precisely, because it looks like an inconsistency and is not. ITBS is provoked by repeated cycling through roughly 20-30 degrees of knee flexion under load, which is what flat and especially downhill running deliver; steep uphill running keeps the knee largely outside that band and has no eccentric braking phase, so it is the one running modality that buys climbing-specific fitness without paying the band. It is still gated on 24 hours of clean walking, with an abort-to-bike rule inside the session, because the argument is mechanistic and this is not the week to test a mechanism against a symptomatic band. Thursday's session is cut rather than cancelled on the same logic: the week lost its eccentric strength block, which was the main justification for a hard day, but 1900m of continuous ascent off the gun at Pirin is still the race's opening demand and it can be rehearsed at zero eccentric cost. The gym block is not merely reduced, it is inverted. Step-downs, split squats and lunges are removed because they load precisely the flexion band that is currently symptomatic, and step-downs in particular were prescribed on 23 August as the centrepiece of the week. Hip abduction, clamshells, single-leg bridges and side planks are retained and promoted, because hip abductor weakness with contralateral pelvic drop is the mechanism that permits the compression, and abductor strengthening is the intervention with the best evidence in ITBS management. Foam-rolling the band itself is explicitly ruled out, since it compresses a structure whose problem is compression; TFL, glutes and vastus lateralis are the targets. The cost is recorded honestly: projected start-line CTL falls from 42.7 to 39.8, roughly two points below the 42 target, with TSB rising to +12.1. That is a real loss of fitness in exchange for a materially better probability of racing at all, and at 38km with 3300m of climbing and a single 1250m descent to finish on seven-hour legs, an athlete two CTL points light will finish and an athlete with active ITBS will not. Confidence is high on the direction and moderate on the magnitude of the deload, since three to four days is a judgement rather than a protocol. The hedge is that Thursday is a genuine decision point with three pre-specified branches rather than a single planned outcome, so a fast resolution restores Saturday's dunes and keeps 5 September's restoration available on ten symptom-free days including running. A physiotherapist appointment is requested this week because the athlete is alone in Milan with time, and hands on the leg resolve in one session what a wellness CSV and a symptom description cannot.

reason: Two findings, and the first one reverses an assumption that has been implicit in this plan for weeks. Whole-activity cadence on 22 August reads 129.8 spm, which looks alarming and is an artefact: 19.4% of that day was spent above 20% gradient at 99 spm, which is hiking, and averaging walking into running produces a number that describes neither. Segmenting the stream by gradient gives the real picture. Descent cadence is 176.6 spm below -20%, 178.9 spm across the second half of the sustained descents, and 176.3 on the final descent, all at or above the 175+ target this plan has been prescribing. His descending technique is not a contributor and the repeated 'cadence 175+' instructions in past sessions were solving a problem he does not have. The deficit is where nobody was looking: 152.1 spm on flat ground and 156.4 spm at -3 to -10%. That matters more than it sounds, because ITBS compression occurs around 20-30 degrees of knee flexion, and slow flat and shallow-downhill running is exactly the regime that holds the knee in that band longest per stride while accumulating the most strides. It is also most of his weekly running, and the final 1250m descent into Bansko is largely runnable gradient rather than the steep hiking terrain where his form is already good. Target set at 165-170 spm, a 5-10% increase, which is the range used in gait-retraining work and which the project's ITBS review cites explicitly alongside step width. Step width is the second lever and cannot be measured from any stream, which is a concrete reason the physiotherapist appointment earns its hour rather than a general one: frontal-plane variables, hip adduction, contralateral pelvic drop and step width are the exact set that a cadence stream cannot see and a person watching him run for five minutes can. Second, the project's evidence review is now applied rather than merely present, and it validates three decisions already taken and contradicts one. It validates the bike (it names cycling or pool work as the Phase 1 fitness maintenance modality), the promotion of hip abductor and extensor work (Sanchez-Alvarado 2024 reports pain reductions up to 100% and function gains up to 57% within 8 weeks, and Fredericson's abductor-weakness finding is the mechanism), and the removal of step-downs, which the review places in Phase 2 at 3-6 weeks rather than Phase 1. It contradicts, or at least does not support, the compressed timeline this plan is running. Phase 1 in the review is one to two weeks of ceased or markedly reduced running; the entry criterion for run-walk is pain-free walking in daily life, stairs and squats for several consecutive days, which he currently fails; and full return to hills and speed is placed at four to six weeks minimum. The race is in 19 days. That conflict is recorded rather than argued away: the plan from here is a compressed, evidence-informed improvisation against a fixed date, not a protocol the literature endorses, and the honest framing is that the deload is being sized to the calendar rather than to the tissue. The 'optimal load' definition is adopted as the governing gate precisely because it is the one part of the framework that survives compression intact: no symptoms during, immediately after, or the next day is a rule that works identically at 19 days and at 19 weeks, and it converts every remaining session into a test with a pre-declared fail condition rather than a judgement call made while warm and optimistic.
